title: Acute Coronary Syndrome: Chest Pain That Cannot Wait
bottomLine: New or changing ischemic symptoms require rapid ACS evaluation. Stop exertion, assess stability, obtain/assist with rapid ECG and ordered biomarkers, give time-sensitive prescribed therapy, and escalate persistent pain, dysrhythmia, heart failure, or hemodynamic instability. Do not dismiss atypical symptoms in women, older adults, or people with diabetes.
recognize: Pressure, heaviness, squeezing, chest/upper-body discomfort, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, unusual fatigue, or syncope can represent ACS
Rest pain, new onset, increasing frequency/severity, or reduced response to the usual angina plan is not stable angina
MI can occur without classic crushing chest pain
assess: Assess pain/onset, vital signs, SpO2, perfusion, heart rhythm, lung sounds, mental status, and associated symptoms
Compare with the patient's usual angina pattern
Reassess pain and hemodynamics after each intervention
actions: Keep the patient at rest and activate the ACS/emergency pathway
Obtain a 12-lead ECG promptly as ordered/protocol permits
Administer prescribed antiplatelet/nitrate/other therapy after safety checks
Prepare for urgent reperfusion/catheterization when indicated by the treatment team
diagnostics: Serial ECGs and cardiac troponin help identify acute myocardial injury/ischemia
A single early negative troponin does not always exclude ACS; timing and serial testing matter
Do not delay emergency response to an unstable patient while waiting for labs
medicationSafety: Aspirin: assess allergy/active major bleeding and administer when ordered/protocol indicates
Nitroglycerin: check blood pressure and recent phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor use; monitor for hypotension
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets increase bleeding risk
teaching: Teach patients not to drive themselves with possible acute MI symptoms; activate EMS according to the emergency plan
Reinforce secondary prevention: medication adherence, smoking cessation, cardiac rehabilitation, lipid/BP/diabetes control
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN recognizes ACS, obtains focused data/ECG when authorized, administers ordered emergency medications within scope, and escalates. Do not independently diagnose STEMI/NSTEMI or decide reperfusion strategy.
examTrap: Giving oxygen automatically to every chest-pain patient despite adequate oxygenation or repeatedly treating changing rest pain as routine stable angina.
oneLinePearl: New chest-pain pattern = ACS until safely evaluated.

title: Heart Failure: Congestion, Perfusion, and Daily Trends
bottomLine: Heart-failure nursing care tracks two questions: is fluid backing up, and is forward perfusion adequate? Trend weight, edema, lung sounds, dyspnea, urine output, blood pressure, renal function, and response to diuresis; escalate acute pulmonary edema, hypotension, severe hypoxemia, or worsening perfusion.
recognize: Congestion: orthopnea, crackles, edema, JVD, rapid weight gain, abdominal fullness
Poor perfusion: cool extremities, confusion, oliguria, hypotension, fatigue
Right- and left-sided findings can overlap; do not reduce the syndrome to one memorized side
assess: Daily weight on the same scale/time when possible
Strict intake/output when ordered, edema, lung sounds, SpO2, heart rate/rhythm, BP, perfusion
Trend potassium, sodium, creatinine, and other ordered labs during diuresis/medication adjustment
actions: Position upright for dyspnea and administer oxygen only when indicated/ordered
Give prescribed diuretic and guideline-directed medications with appropriate checks
Monitor urine output, symptoms, BP, renal function/electrolytes, and escalate poor response
diagnostics: BNP/NT-proBNP can support HF assessment but must be interpreted with clinical context
Echocardiography defines ventricular function/structure
Chest imaging can show congestion/other causes of dyspnea
medicationSafety: Loop diuretics: monitor volume status, potassium/magnesium, renal function, BP
ACE inhibitor/ARB/ARNI: monitor BP, potassium, renal function; pregnancy risk matters
Beta blockers: monitor HR/BP and do not abruptly stop without a plan
SGLT2 inhibitors: watch volume status and sick-day/perioperative guidance
teaching: Daily weights and symptom action plan
Medication adherence and sodium/fluid guidance as prescribed
Report rapid worsening weight/dyspnea/edema based on the individualized plan
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN trends congestion/perfusion, administers ordered therapy, reinforces the HF plan, and reports deterioration. Do not independently change diuretic or guideline-directed doses unless an authorized protocol permits it.
examTrap: Focusing only on edema while missing hypotension, confusion, or oliguria that indicate poor forward perfusion.
oneLinePearl: HF: watch both backup and output—congestion and perfusion.

title: Cardiogenic Shock: The Failing Pump and Falling Perfusion
bottomLine: Cardiogenic shock is pump failure with inadequate tissue perfusion, often after large MI or severe cardiac dysfunction. Hypotension plus cool/clammy skin, altered mentation, oliguria, rising lactate, pulmonary congestion, or worsening rhythm requires immediate escalation and advanced hemodynamic support.
recognize: Hypotension or narrowing pulse pressure
Cool mottled extremities, delayed capillary refill, confusion, oliguria
Crackles/pulmonary edema can coexist with systemic hypoperfusion
assess: Continuous vital signs/rhythm, perfusion, mental status, urine output, SpO2, lung sounds
Trend response to vasoactive/inotropic therapy and mechanical support if used
Watch for recurrent ischemia and dysrhythmias
actions: Activate rapid/emergency response and maintain prescribed oxygen/airway support
Administer ordered vasoactive/inotropic medications via the required monitoring pathway
Prepare for urgent reperfusion/mechanical circulatory support decisions by the advanced team
diagnostics: ECG/troponin identify ischemic cause when present
Echo evaluates ventricular/mechanical complications
Lactate, renal/liver markers, blood gas, and hemodynamic data trend end-organ perfusion
medicationSafety: Vasoactive drugs can cause ischemia/dysrhythmia and require close BP/rhythm/perfusion monitoring
Large uncritical fluid boluses can worsen pulmonary edema in pump failure; fluid decisions are hemodynamic and ordered
teaching: Family teaching is secondary to stabilization; explain devices/therapies briefly and clearly when possible
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN may care for shock patients only where role, competency, and setting allow. Do not independently titrate advanced vasoactive infusions or mechanical support unless explicitly authorized; recognize deterioration and escalate immediately.
examTrap: Giving repeated large fluid boluses simply because blood pressure is low without considering pump failure and pulmonary congestion.
oneLinePearl: Shock = perfusion problem; cardiogenic shock = the pump cannot move the blood forward.

title: Atrial Fibrillation: Rate, Perfusion, and Stroke Prevention
bottomLine: With atrial fibrillation, first determine stability and ventricular response. Unstable tachyarrhythmia with hypotension, ischemic chest discomfort, shock, acute heart failure, or altered mental status requires emergency escalation; stable care focuses on rate/rhythm strategy and thromboembolic risk as ordered.
recognize: Irregularly irregular pulse/rhythm, palpitations, fatigue, dyspnea, dizziness; some patients are asymptomatic
Rapid ventricular response can reduce filling and cardiac output
AF increases embolic stroke risk; anticoagulation decisions depend on individualized risk/benefit
assess: Rate/rhythm, BP/perfusion, chest pain, dyspnea, mental status, neurologic findings
Check medication adherence, bleeding, and ordered electrolytes/thyroid or other contributors
Reassess after rate-control medications
actions: Escalate unstable AF immediately and prepare for synchronized cardioversion per emergency plan
Administer ordered rate/rhythm medications and anticoagulants
Monitor for stroke symptoms and bleeding
diagnostics: 12-lead ECG confirms rhythm
Electrolytes, thyroid tests, echo, and other studies identify contributors/structure
Do not diagnose a stroke-free state just because AF symptoms improve
medicationSafety: Beta blockers/diltiazem/verapamil can cause bradycardia/hypotension and have patient-specific contraindications
Anticoagulants require bleeding monitoring and adherence; drug choice/dose depends on renal function and indication
redFlags: Very rapid rate with poor perfusion
teaching: Teach pulse/symptom monitoring as prescribed, anticoagulant adherence, bleeding precautions, and stroke warning signs
Do not stop anticoagulation because the rhythm feels normal unless the authorized clinician changes the plan
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN identifies irregular/rate changes, obtains ECG when authorized, gives ordered medications, monitors response/bleeding, and escalates. Cardioversion/anticoagulation strategy is not an independent PN decision.
examTrap: Focusing on the rhythm strip while ignoring that the patient is hypotensive, confused, or in acute pulmonary edema.
oneLinePearl: AF question one: stable or unstable? Question two: rate and stroke protection.

title: SVT: Fast Rhythm, First Check Stability
bottomLine: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia becomes an emergency when it causes hypotension, shock, ischemic discomfort, acute heart failure, or altered mental status. Stable SVT may be treated with vagal maneuvers and medications under protocol; unstable SVT requires urgent synchronized cardioversion preparation.
recognize: Abrupt rapid regular palpitations, possible dyspnea/chest discomfort/dizziness
Rate may be very fast with narrow complexes, though rhythm diagnosis belongs to the qualified clinician/team
Symptoms matter more than the number alone
assess: BP/perfusion, mental status, chest pain, dyspnea, SpO2, rhythm
Obtain 12-lead ECG if it does not delay treatment
Check IV access and resuscitation readiness when medications/cardioversion are planned
actions: Escalate unstable tachycardia and prepare for synchronized cardioversion
For stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia, assist with ordered/authorized vagal maneuvers and medication pathway
Reassess rhythm and hemodynamics after intervention
diagnostics: ECG differentiates SVT from atrial flutter, AF, sinus tachycardia, or wide-complex rhythms
Evaluate precipitating causes such as stimulant use, electrolyte disturbance, fever, hypovolemia, or thyroid disease as ordered
medicationSafety: Adenosine is given by rapid IV push followed immediately by flush under monitored emergency protocol; transient flushing/chest pressure and brief asystole can occur
Do not give adenosine casually for an irregular or uncertain wide-complex rhythm
teaching: Reinforce trigger reduction and follow-up for recurrent episodes according to the care plan
scopeAndDelegation: Medication administration such as adenosine and cardioversion roles depend on state/facility policy and emergency protocols. The PN/LVN's universal responsibility is rapid recognition, monitoring, and escalation.
examTrap: Trying repeated vagal maneuvers in a hypotensive confused patient instead of treating the rhythm as unstable.
oneLinePearl: Fast rhythm + unstable patient = electricity pathway, not delay.

title: Ventricular Tachycardia and Fibrillation: Pulse or No Pulse Changes Everything
bottomLine: With a wide-complex ventricular rhythm, assess the patient and pulse immediately. Pulseless VT/VF is cardiac arrest: activate the response, begin high-quality CPR, and defibrillate as soon as available per the 2025 AHA algorithm. VT with a pulse follows the stable-versus-unstable tachycardia pathway.
recognize: VF: chaotic ventricular electrical activity with no effective pulse
Pulseless VT: organized wide-complex tachycardia without a pulse
VT with pulse can still cause hypotension, ischemia, heart failure, or altered mental status
assess: Check responsiveness, breathing, and pulse rapidly when a lethal rhythm appears
Verify electrode/lead connection only if the patient is clearly stable; never troubleshoot the monitor while an unresponsive pulseless patient waits
After ROSC, assess airway/oxygenation, BP/perfusion, rhythm, neurologic status
actions: Pulseless VT/VF: CPR + defibrillation + ACLS medications/causes per emergency team
Unstable VT with pulse: prepare for synchronized cardioversion
Stable wide-complex tachycardia: monitored expert evaluation and ordered antiarrhythmic therapy
diagnostics: ECG/rhythm analysis guides treatment; electrolytes, ischemia evaluation, and reversible-cause workup follow stabilization
medicationSafety: Epinephrine and antiarrhythmics are protocol-driven in cardiac arrest
Amiodarone and other antiarrhythmics can cause hypotension/bradycardia/QT effects; monitor closely
teaching: After recovery, reinforce medication/device follow-up and emergency-response education as part of the discharge plan
scopeAndDelegation: All trained staff should respond to cardiac arrest according to certification and facility protocol. PN/LVN medication/defibrillation roles depend on training and policy, but CPR/AED/emergency activation must not be delayed by title uncertainty.
examTrap: Seeing VT on the monitor and choosing an antiarrhythmic before checking whether the patient has a pulse.
oneLinePearl: VT? Touch the patient—pulse first, algorithm second.
sourceBasis: 2025 AHA CPR/ECC Adult Cardiac Arrest and Tachyarrhythmia Algorithms

title: Bradycardia and Heart Block: Treat the Patient, Not the Rate Alone
bottomLine: A slow rate is urgent when it produces hypotension, altered mental status, ischemic discomfort, shock, or acute heart failure. Symptomatic bradycardia requires rapid escalation, identification of reversible causes, and preparation for atropine/pacing or other treatment per protocol.
recognize: Dizziness, syncope, weakness, hypotension, chest discomfort, dyspnea, confusion
High-grade AV block can cause sudden hemodynamic compromise
Athletic or medication-related bradycardia may be asymptomatic and not require emergency treatment
assess: Rate/rhythm, pulse quality, BP/perfusion, mental status, chest pain, lung sounds
Review beta blockers, calcium-channel blockers, digoxin, antiarrhythmics, recent MI, electrolytes
Obtain ECG and IV access as ordered without delaying response
actions: Escalate symptomatic bradycardia
Administer atropine if ordered/protocol appropriate and monitor response
Prepare for transcutaneous pacing and vasoactive support when needed
diagnostics: 12-lead ECG helps identify sinus bradycardia versus AV block
Electrolytes, drug levels, ischemia workup, and other tests target reversible causes
medicationSafety: Hold/clarify rate-slowing medications when ordered parameters are not met
Atropine may be ineffective in some high-grade blocks; do not delay pacing/escalation in a deteriorating patient
teaching: Teach pulse/symptom checks and when to seek urgent help if the patient takes rate-slowing drugs or has a pacemaker
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN recognizes abnormal rate/rhythm and perfusion, holds/administers medications according to explicit parameters/orders, and escalates. Pacing and advanced vasoactive management require trained authorized personnel.
examTrap: Treating every heart rate below 60 as an emergency or, conversely, ignoring a rate of 48 in a hypotensive confused patient.
oneLinePearl: Bradycardia is a perfusion question, not just a number.

title: Severe Hypertension: Is There Acute Target-Organ Injury?
bottomLine: A very high blood pressure becomes a hypertensive emergency when it is accompanied by acute target-organ injury such as encephalopathy, stroke symptoms, ACS, pulmonary edema, aortic syndrome, or acute kidney injury. Recheck technique, assess symptoms/organ injury, and escalate; do not rapidly lower asymptomatic chronic severe hypertension on your own.
recognize: Emergency cues: neurologic deficits/confusion/seizure, ischemic chest pain, acute dyspnea/pulmonary edema, tearing chest/back pain, severe pregnancy-related features, worsening renal function
A single elevated reading can be affected by pain, anxiety, bladder distention, cuff size, or technique
Rapid BP reduction can itself impair organ perfusion
assess: Repeat BP with correct cuff/position, compare arms when clinically relevant and not delaying care
Assess neuro status, chest pain, dyspnea, vision, urine output, pregnancy/postpartum status, medication adherence/substances
Trend response to ordered therapy closely
actions: Escalate suspected hypertensive emergency
Administer ordered IV/oral antihypertensives and monitor for excessive BP drop
Treat accompanying emergency syndrome under protocol
diagnostics: ECG/troponin, renal tests/urinalysis, neuro imaging, chest/aortic imaging, or pregnancy labs are driven by symptoms
Do not call severe BP an emergency solely from the number without assessing acute organ injury
medicationSafety: IV antihypertensives require close monitoring
Avoid doubling missed chronic doses unless specifically directed
Abrupt withdrawal of some agents such as clonidine/beta blockers can cause rebound or adverse effects
teaching: Reinforce adherence, home BP technique, and specific emergency symptoms; asymptomatic readings still need follow-up according to the plan
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN verifies BP accuracy, performs focused assessment, administers ordered treatment, and escalates organ-injury symptoms. Diagnosis and BP-reduction targets are provider/team decisions.
examTrap: Trying to normalize a severely elevated BP as fast as possible without assessing whether acute organ injury is present.
oneLinePearl: Hypertensive emergency = high pressure plus acute organ injury.

title: Deep Vein Thrombosis: Protect the Limb, Prevent the Embolus
bottomLine: Suspect DVT with new unilateral swelling, pain/tenderness, warmth, or color change in a patient with VTE risk. Do not massage the limb or use Homan sign. Escalate new chest pain, dyspnea, syncope, or hypoxemia immediately for possible PE.
recognize: Risk: immobility/surgery, prior VTE, cancer, pregnancy/postpartum, estrogen, trauma, thrombophilia
DVT can be asymptomatic; absence of classic signs does not exclude it
Bilateral edema from heart/renal disease is a different pattern than new asymmetric limb findings
assess: Compare limb swelling, warmth, color, pain, and pulses without aggressive manipulation
Assess respiratory symptoms for embolization
Monitor bleeding and platelet/renal parameters as required by the anticoagulant plan
actions: Notify the responsible clinician for new suspected DVT and follow mobility/compression instructions
Administer prescribed anticoagulant
Use VTE prevention: mobility, hydration when appropriate, compression/prophylaxis as ordered
diagnostics: Compression ultrasonography is a standard diagnostic test
D-dimer can help exclude VTE in selected low-probability settings but is nonspecific when elevated
medicationSafety: Heparin/LMWH/DOAC/warfarin all increase bleeding risk but have different monitoring, interaction, renal, and reversal considerations
Warfarin is monitored with INR; heparin monitoring depends on product/protocol
redFlags: Limb threatened by severe swelling/perfusion change
teaching: Anticoagulant adherence and bleeding precautions
Avoid massaging a suspected DVT
Know PE warning signs
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN recognizes findings, supports prescribed mobility/anticoagulation, monitors bleeding, and reports PE symptoms urgently. Do not diagnose DVT by bedside maneuver.
examTrap: Performing Homan sign or massaging the painful calf to 'improve circulation.'
oneLinePearl: New one-sided swelling: think clot; new dyspnea: think embolus.

title: Acute Limb Ischemia: The Six Ps Are a Time Warning
bottomLine: Sudden limb pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, or poikilothermia/coolness suggests acute arterial ischemia. Motor or sensory loss indicates a threatened limb: keep it protected, perform rapid neurovascular comparison, and obtain urgent vascular escalation.
recognize: Abrupt severe limb pain/coolness/color change
Loss of pulse/Doppler signal
Paresthesia or paralysis implies advanced ischemia
assess: Compare both limbs: pulses/Doppler, cap refill, color, temperature, sensation, movement
Mark/document pulse sites when required and trend changes
Assess for AF/embolism history, vascular procedures, grafts, anticoagulation
actions: Urgent vascular/surgical escalation
Protect the limb from pressure, heat, or trauma
Administer ordered anticoagulation and prepare for revascularization
diagnostics: Doppler and vascular imaging define perfusion/occlusion
Do not let nonessential testing delay salvage of a threatened limb
medicationSafety: Unfractionated heparin is commonly used when not contraindicated; monitor bleeding and protocol-specific labs
teaching: For chronic PAD, reinforce smoking cessation, foot protection, exercise/medication plan; acute sudden changes require emergency evaluation
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN performs focused neurovascular assessment, protects the limb, administers ordered therapy, and escalates. Revascularization decisions are vascular-team decisions.
examTrap: Applying a heating pad to an ischemic numb foot or elevating an acutely ischemic limb high above the heart.
oneLinePearl: Acute arterial loss is limb time—pain plus neuro change is urgent.
sourceBasis: 2024 ACC/AHA Lower Extremity Peripheral Artery Disease Guideline

title: Aortic Dissection: Sudden Pain Plus Pulse or Neuro Change
bottomLine: Abrupt severe chest/back/abdominal pain with pulse deficit, neurologic symptoms, syncope, new aortic-regurgitation findings, or malperfusion is acute aortic syndrome until proven otherwise. Keep the patient at rest, monitor closely, and escalate for rapid imaging/anti-impulse/surgical evaluation; do not automatically anticoagulate every chest-pain patient before considering dissection.
recognize: Abrupt maximal-at-onset pain may radiate/migrate
Unequal pulses/BP, stroke-like deficits, limb ischemia, abdominal ischemia, syncope
Proximal dissection can cause tamponade, acute aortic regurgitation, MI, or rupture
assess: ABCs, BP/HR, perfusion, neuro status, pulses/limb temperature, pain
Compare bilateral BP/pulses only when it will not delay emergency care
Monitor urine output and signs of organ malperfusion
actions: Emergency vascular/cardiothoracic escalation
Maintain rest/continuous monitoring
Administer ordered beta blockade/analgesia/vasodilator sequence under close hemodynamic monitoring
Prepare for emergent surgery for appropriate proximal dissections
diagnostics: CT angiography commonly diagnoses stable patients; TEE may be used when instability/logistics require
ECG/troponin can be abnormal and may mimic ACS
medicationSafety: Rate control generally precedes pure vasodilation to reduce shear
Anticoagulation/antiplatelet therapy may be harmful if the true cause is dissection with bleeding risk—follow the confirmed emergency pathway
teaching: Long-term survivors need strict BP control, surveillance imaging, and emergency evaluation for recurrent sudden symptoms
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN recognizes the pattern, keeps the patient monitored/resting, administers ordered therapy within scope, and escalates immediately. Imaging/surgical and anti-impulse targets are team-directed.
examTrap: Treating all severe chest pain as routine ACS and giving anticoagulation before recognizing pulse/neuro findings suggesting dissection.
oneLinePearl: Sudden severe pain + pulse/neuro difference = think aorta fast.

title: Cardiac Tamponade: Falling Filling, Falling Output
bottomLine: Tamponade is hemodynamic compromise from pressure around the heart. Trend tachycardia, falling BP/pulse pressure, rising JVP, dyspnea, muffled heart sounds when present, oliguria, confusion, and poor perfusion—especially after cardiac procedures/trauma—and escalate urgently for bedside imaging and drainage.
recognize: Beck triad may be incomplete; do not wait for all classic signs
Rapidly accumulating smaller effusions can be more dangerous than slowly accumulating large ones
Post-procedure sudden deterioration is a major clue
assess: BP trend, HR/rhythm, JVP, heart/lung sounds, pulses, mental status, urine output/perfusion
Assess procedure history, trauma, anticoagulation, malignancy, renal/pericardial disease
Watch for pulsus paradoxus if measured by trained staff
actions: Urgent emergency/cardiology escalation
Prepare for echocardiography and pericardiocentesis/surgical drainage
Maintain continuous monitoring and prescribed supportive measures while definitive treatment is arranged
diagnostics: Echocardiography is key to identifying effusion and tamponade physiology
ECG may show low voltage/electrical alternans but absence does not rule it out
medicationSafety: Preload-reducing drugs can worsen hemodynamics in tamponade; medication decisions are ordered and context-specific
Anticoagulation can worsen bleeding-related effusion and requires urgent review
teaching: After treatment, reinforce follow-up and recurrence symptoms according to the cause
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN's essential role is trend recognition, continuous monitoring, preparation/support for emergency intervention, and immediate escalation—not diagnosing tamponade from a single sign.
examTrap: Waiting for Beck triad to be complete before reporting a post-procedure patient whose BP is falling and JVP is rising.
oneLinePearl: Tamponade is a trend toward obstructed filling and poor perfusion.
sourceBasis: AHA/ACC pericardial emergency evidence and echocardiography standards

title: Infective Endocarditis: Fever Plus a High-Risk Heart Story
bottomLine: Think infective endocarditis with persistent fever/systemic illness plus prosthetic valve, prior endocarditis, certain congenital disease, injection-drug exposure, intracardiac device, or compatible embolic/cardiac findings. Obtain ordered blood cultures before antibiotics when feasible and the patient is stable, then give prolonged antimicrobial therapy exactly as ordered and watch for embolic, valve, heart-failure, and neurologic complications.
recognize: Fever, chills, fatigue, new/changing murmur, petechiae or embolic phenomena
Stroke, splenic/renal infarct, limb ischemia, or heart failure can be complications
Prosthetic material or bacteremia increases concern
assess: Temperature, heart sounds, HF signs, neuro status, skin/embolic findings, perfusion
Inspect IV access and monitor long-course antimicrobial complications
Assess substance-use needs without stigma when relevant
actions: Collect ordered blood cultures correctly before first antibiotic when this does not delay emergency therapy
Administer IV antibiotics on schedule
Escalate new neurologic deficit, HF, conduction change, or embolic symptoms
Maintain line-infection prevention
diagnostics: Multiple blood cultures and echocardiography are central to diagnosis
Do not interpret one negative culture as excluding endocarditis after prior antibiotics or with high suspicion
medicationSafety: Long IV antimicrobial courses require renal/hepatic, CBC, drug-level, hearing, or other monitoring depending on agent
Report rash, diarrhea, renal decline, hearing/vestibular symptoms, or line complications
teaching: Complete the full antimicrobial course and keep follow-up/echo appointments
Only selected high-risk cardiac patients need antibiotic prophylaxis for certain procedures; do not teach universal prophylaxis
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN monitors and administers ordered prolonged therapy, reinforces line care and adherence, and recognizes complications. Antibiotic selection and surgical indications are team decisions.
examTrap: Teaching that every patient with a heart murmur needs prophylactic antibiotics before dental work.
oneLinePearl: Endocarditis harms by infection, valve destruction, and emboli—watch all three.

title: Pacemakers and ICDs: Capture, Sensing, and the Unstable Patient
bottomLine: A paced rhythm must produce mechanical perfusion. If pacing spikes are not followed by expected depolarization or the patient is dizzy, hypotensive, syncopal, or bradycardic, assess the patient and escalate. Recurrent ICD shocks, especially with symptoms, require urgent evaluation.
recognize: Failure to capture: pacing stimulus without expected depolarization
Failure to sense can cause inappropriate pacing behavior
Device infection can present with pocket redness/drainage, fever, or bacteremia
assess: Pulse/perfusion, BP, symptoms, rhythm/telemetry, incision/pocket after implantation
Correlate electrical rate with palpable pulse
Ask about number/timing of ICD shocks and associated syncope/chest pain
actions: Escalate symptomatic device malfunction
Maintain telemetry and prepare for external pacing/defibrillation support if unstable
Follow post-implant arm/activity and wound instructions from the procedural plan
diagnostics: 12-lead ECG and device interrogation evaluate function
Chest imaging may assess lead position after implantation when ordered
medicationSafety: Antiarrhythmics/rate-control drugs can interact with underlying bradyarrhythmia/device dependence; monitor HR/BP and symptoms
teaching: Carry device identification and keep device follow-up
Follow manufacturer/clinic guidance for electromagnetic interference; everyday electronics are not universally prohibited
Report shocks, syncope, infection signs, or new palpitations per the plan
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN recognizes malfunction/infection, monitors perfusion, and escalates. Device programming/interrogation is performed by qualified personnel.
examTrap: Seeing pacer spikes on the monitor and assuming the patient is perfusing without checking the pulse and symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Electrical pacing only counts when the patient captures and perfuses.
sourceBasis: AHA/HRS cardiac implantable electronic device guidance

title: Cardiac Catheterization and CABG: The Complications You Must Catch Early
bottomLine: After cardiac catheterization or CABG, trend perfusion and procedure-specific complications: access-site bleeding/hematoma and distal circulation after cath; bleeding, tamponade, dysrhythmia, low cardiac output, respiratory complications, and graft ischemia after surgery. Sudden hypotension, chest pain, neuro change, or major bleeding is never routine recovery.
recognize: Cath: bleeding/hematoma, retroperitoneal bleed, loss of distal pulse, contrast kidney injury, allergic reaction
CABG: excessive bleeding, tamponade, AF/other dysrhythmias, low output, atelectasis/pneumonia, wound infection
New ischemic symptoms after revascularization require urgent evaluation
assess: Cath: access site, distal pulse/color/temp/sensation, BP/HR, pain, urine output
CABG: chest-tube output, hemodynamics, rhythm, lung sounds/oxygenation, incision, neuro status, urine output
Trend hemoglobin/renal function/electrolytes as ordered
actions: Maintain prescribed access-site positioning/restrictions and respond to bleeding with direct pressure/emergency protocol
After CABG, support pulmonary hygiene, early mobility, pain control, glucose/temperature management per plan
Escalate sudden high chest-tube output or sudden cessation with deterioration
diagnostics: ECG/troponin, CBC, renal/electrolyte tests, imaging, and hemodynamics are selected based on procedure and symptoms
medicationSafety: Antiplatelet/anticoagulant therapy increases bleeding risk but may be essential for graft/stent protection—never stop independently
Metformin/contrast and renal considerations follow current order/policy rather than a universal outdated hold rule
teaching: Access-site activity/wound instructions, hydration when appropriate, medication adherence after stenting
CABG: sternal/wound care, activity progression, cardiac rehabilitation, infection/ischemia warning signs
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN performs focused post-procedure monitoring and ordered care within unit scope, and escalates complications. Sheath removal, titrated infusions, and some post-open-heart care may be restricted by policy/state competency.
examTrap: Treating a growing groin hematoma after femoral cath as expected bruising or clamping a mediastinal chest tube because drainage seems high.
oneLinePearl: After revascularization, bleeding and perfusion are your early-warning pair.
